terms.grammar: adverb, before the word it negates; with the verb, usually just before it
evidence: Ter. And. 194: Dāvus sum, nōn Oedipūs.
Hor. Ep. 1.14.36: nec lūsisse pudet, sed nōn incīdere lūdum
terms.comment: The negative of statements and questions. “And not” is nec; “not even”, nē … quidem; “not yet”, nōndum. A double negative makes a positive: nōn nēmō, somebody; nōn nihil, something.

terms.grammar: adverb: in classical prose mostly with adverbs and adjectives; with verbs freely in comedy
evidence: Tac. Agr. 9.7: haud semper errat fāma
Ter. Ad. 373–374: Hem, Dēmea, haud aspexeram tē.
terms.comment: In Cicero with a verb only in haud sciō an and haud dubitō (Lewis & Short); otherwise haud multō post, haud facile, haud secus.

terms.grammar: adverb and conjunction, with the subjunctive; with the imperative in comedy and poetry
evidence: Sen. Ep. 13.4: nē sīs miser ante tempus
Plaut. Mil. 1345: Nē timē, voluptās mea.
terms.comment: The negative of the will: “don’t …!”, “may it not …”, “so that … not”. Prose forbids with nōlī + infinitive or nē + perfect subjunctive (nē admīserīs).

phrases.english: there’s no shame in having played, only in not breaking the game off
